subject: biology
title: Reflex actions and synapses
summary: Trace the reflex arc, explain how impulses cross a synapse, and classify reflexes as spinal, cranial or conditioned.
objectives: Define a reflex action and give its main features
Trace the reflex arc from receptor to effector
Explain how an impulse crosses a synapse
Distinguish between spinal, cranial and conditioned reflexes

sections.title: Faster than thinking
sections.body:
You are walking barefoot across a field and step on a sharp thorn. Your foot lifts off the ground before you even feel the pain. You did not decide to move. It just happened.

This is a reflex action: a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that happens without conscious thought. Reflexes protect the body from harm, such as burns, cuts or dust in the eye.
bullets: Rapid: faster than a thought-out response

sections.title: The spinal cord
sections.body:
The spinal cord is part of the CNS. It runs from the base of the brain down the back, protected inside the bones of the vertebral column (backbone).

The spinal cord has two jobs. It carries impulses up to the brain and down from the brain. It also handles many reflexes by itself, without waiting for the brain.

sections.title: The reflex arc
sections.body:
The pathway an impulse follows during a reflex is called the reflex arc. The diagram shows the reflex that pulls your hand away from a hot iron.

Notice that the impulse goes into the spinal cord and straight back out again. It does not have to travel all the way up to the brain and back, and that is why the reflex is so fast. A separate impulse does travel up to the brain, which is why you feel the pain a moment later.

sections.question: What is the correct order of a reflex arc?
options: Receptor, motor neurone, relay neurone, sensory neurone, effector
Receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector
Effector, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, receptor
Receptor, relay neurone, motor neurone, sensory neurone, effector
sections.explanation: The receptor detects the stimulus first, the sensory neurone carries the impulse into the spinal cord, the relay neurone links to the motor neurone, and the effector responds. Putting the motor neurone before the sensory neurone would mean the response comes before the message arrives.

sections.title: Worked example: tracing a reflex pathway
sections.problem: Mwila picks up a hot iron by mistake and drops it at once. Describe the reflex arc involved, naming the stimulus, receptor, each neurone and the effector.
steps: Step 1: Stimulus = heat from the iron.
Step 2: Receptor = heat and pain receptors in the skin of the hand. They start an impulse.
Step 3: A sensory neurone carries the impulse to the spinal cord.
Step 4: In the spinal cord, a relay neurone passes the impulse to a motor neurone.
Step 5: The motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector, a muscle in the arm.
Step 6: The muscle contracts and the hand lets go and moves away. This is the response. Only afterwards does the brain receive a message and Mwila feels the pain.
sections.answer: Heat, skin receptors, sensory neurone, relay neurone (spinal cord), motor neurone, arm muscle contracts. The brain is told after the response.

sections.title: Synapses: crossing the gap
sections.body:
Neurones do not touch each other. Between the end of one neurone and the next there is a tiny gap. The junction is called a synapse, and the gap is the synaptic gap.

An electrical impulse cannot jump the gap. Instead, when the impulse reaches the axon ending, small sacs called vesicles release a chemical called a neurotransmitter. It diffuses across the gap and attaches to receptors on the next neurone. This starts a new impulse in that neurone.
bullets: Electrical impulse arrives at the axon ending
Vesicles release neurotransmitter into the gap
Neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds to receptors
A new impulse starts in the next neurone

sections.question: Why can impulses cross a synapse in one direction only?
options: The gap is too wide on one side
Only the axon ending releases neurotransmitter, and only the next neurone has receptors for it
Myelin blocks the impulse going backwards
sections.explanation: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are only on the sending side, and receptors are only on the receiving side, so the message can only go forwards. Myelin covers the axon; it has nothing to do with the synapse.

sections.title: Spinal and cranial reflexes
sections.body:
Reflexes are grouped by where in the CNS the impulse is processed.

In a spinal reflex, the spinal cord handles the impulse. Examples are pulling your hand from a hot object and the knee-jerk reflex. The knee-jerk is a very short arc: the sensory neurone connects directly to the motor neurone in the spinal cord.

In a cranial reflex, the brain handles the impulse, and it travels along cranial nerves (nerves joined to the brain). Examples are blinking, coughing, sneezing and the pupil reflex. These are still automatic: you do not choose to do them.

sections.title: Worked example: the pupil reflex
sections.problem: Thandiwe walks out of a dark classroom into bright midday sunshine. Her pupils quickly become smaller. Explain this reflex.
steps: Step 1: Stimulus = a sudden increase in light intensity.
Step 2: Receptor = light-sensitive cells in the retina of the eye.
Step 3: A sensory neurone in the optic nerve carries impulses to the brain. This makes it a cranial reflex.
Step 4: The brain sends impulses along motor neurones to the iris.
Step 5: Effector = the muscles of the iris. The circular muscles contract and the radial muscles relax.
Step 6: Response = the pupil gets smaller, so less light enters and the retina is protected from damage.
sections.answer: Bright light is detected by the retina; impulses go to the brain and back to the iris; the circular muscles contract and the pupil narrows, letting in less light.

sections.title: Conditioned reflexes
sections.body:
Spinal and cranial reflexes are inborn: you have them from birth. A conditioned reflex is different. It is learned by repeated association.

The scientist Ivan Pavlov showed this with dogs. Food made the dogs produce saliva (an inborn reflex). Pavlov rang a bell every time just before giving food. After many repeats, the bell alone made the dogs produce saliva. The bell had become a conditioned stimulus, and the saliva was now a conditioned response.

You have conditioned reflexes too. If your mouth waters when you hear kapenta frying in the kitchen, you have learned to link that sound with food.

sections.title: Common mistake: saying the brain controls a spinal reflex
sections.body:
Students often write that "the brain sends a message to the muscle" in a spinal reflex. This is wrong. In a spinal reflex the response comes from the spinal cord, before the brain is involved. The brain is only told afterwards, which is why you feel the pain after you have already moved.

In exams, always name the spinal cord as the place where the sensory, relay and motor neurones connect.

sections.question: Every day the school bell rings for lunch, and Bupe's mouth starts to water even before she sees any food. What type of reflex is this?
sections.explanation: Bupe has learned to link the bell with food through daily repetition, just like Pavlov's dogs. That makes it a conditioned reflex. A cranial reflex such as blinking is inborn, not learned.

sections.title: Key points
bullets: A reflex action is rapid, automatic and protective, and needs no conscious thought.
Reflex arc: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
At a synapse, neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap, so impulses pass one way only.
Spinal reflexes are processed in the spinal cord; cranial reflexes (blinking, coughing, pupil reflex) in the brain.
Conditioned reflexes are learned by repeated association, as in Pavlov's dogs.

quiz.question: In a spinal reflex, where is the impulse passed from the sensory neurone to the motor neurone?
quiz.explanation: In a spinal reflex the connection is made in the spinal cord. The brain receives a message later, but it is not part of the reflex arc itself.

quiz.question: Which of these is a cranial reflex?
options: Pulling the hand from a hot pot
Salivating at the sound of a bell
quiz.explanation: In the pupil reflex, impulses are processed in the brain, so it is a cranial reflex. The knee-jerk and pulling away from heat are spinal reflexes, and salivating at a bell is a conditioned reflex.

quiz.question: In Pavlov's experiment, what was the bell after conditioning was complete?
quiz.explanation: Before conditioning the bell was a neutral stimulus. After repeated pairing with food, the bell alone caused salivation, so it became a conditioned stimulus. The salivation was the conditioned response.

quiz.question: A learner pricks a finger on a pin and pulls the hand back. Which neurone carries the impulse from the skin to the spinal cord?
quiz.explanation: Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors towards the CNS. Motor neurones carry them away from the CNS, and relay neurones work inside the spinal cord.

quiz.question: What is the effector in the pupil reflex?
quiz.explanation: The iris muscles carry out the response by changing the size of the pupil. The retina contains the receptors and the optic nerve carries the sensory impulse, so neither is the effector.

quiz.question: How does a nerve impulse pass from one neurone to the next across a synapse?
options: The electrical impulse jumps straight across the gap
The two neurones touch and the impulse flows through
Myelin carries the impulse across the gap
A neurotransmitter chemical diffuses across the gap
quiz.explanation: The impulse makes vesicles release a neurotransmitter, which diffuses across the synaptic gap and binds to receptors on the next neurone, starting a new impulse. The neurones do not touch, and electricity cannot jump the gap.

quiz.question: What makes a conditioned reflex different from a spinal or cranial reflex?
options: It is learned through repeated association
It does not use the nervous system
It is processed in the spinal cord only
quiz.explanation: Conditioned reflexes are learned from experience, while spinal and cranial reflexes are inborn. Conditioned reflexes still use the nervous system, mainly the brain.

quiz.question: Why do you usually pull your hand away from a hot object BEFORE you feel the pain?
options: Pain receptors are slower than heat receptors
The muscles act without any nerve impulse
The response is sent from the spinal cord before the message reaches the brain
The brain decides to move first and feel later
quiz.explanation: The reflex arc runs through the spinal cord, a short route, so the muscle responds quickly. The message about pain has to travel further, up to the brain, so the feeling comes a moment later. The brain does not make the decision in a spinal reflex.

glossary.definition: A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that happens without conscious thought.
The pathway of an impulse in a reflex: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
The junction between two neurones, including the tiny gap between them.
A chemical released at a synapse that carries the message across the gap.
A reflex in which the impulse is processed in the spinal cord, for example the knee-jerk.
A reflex in which the impulse is processed in the brain, for example blinking.
A reflex that is learned by repeatedly linking a new stimulus with a natural one.
